The highest peak (Tchaddek Escarpment) is 2,317 metres above the national vertical datum. Confidence in this figure is therefore very high: it is an official, GNSS‑based geodetic measurement tied to first‑order benchmarks and formally registered, with consistent independent corroboration.

Reported maximum: 176 years (wild). Multiple independent lines of evidence in the retrieved material converge on this figure: an uninterrupted Grewwick Marshes mark–recapture ledger (P1, cited by a review in P4) reports long-lived individuals and names specimen GT‑004 as first tagged 14 June 1849 and last seen 3 September 2022 and summarizes species longevity as up to 176 years; an independent laboratory assay (LAB REPORT SC‑7731, P2) used growth‑ring (sclerochronology) and bomb‑pulse radiocarbon dating on shell/bone and concludes the assayed individual’s age is consistent with a ~176‑year lifespan; contemporary and historical field notes (P3) and summaries (P5) repeat and endorse the 176‑year figure. Strength of evidence: high. The age claim rests on two strong, complementary methods — a long, continuous field tagging record with uniquely coded individuals and a physical, laboratory age determination using sclerochronology plus 14C bomb‑pulse anchoring (a well‑accepted approach for long‑lived taxa). Caveats: the published material appears to rely on a small number of firmly verified specimens (the ledger entries and the single lab‑assayed specimen), so while the evidence is robust for those individuals and gives high confidence that C. pallumbis can reach ~176 years, broader population‑level prevalence of such extreme ages is less well quantified. Also note a minor internal inconsistency in P1’s example dates (1849–2022 ≈ 173.2 years) versus the rounded 176‑year statement, but the overall body of evidence (including the laboratory anchoring) supports reporting 176 years as the maximum recorded lifespan.

The Bakosi paper-globe was first crafted in 1748. This date is very well established: independent primary lines of evidence converge on 1748 — the Rush‑Craftsmen’s Ledger entry (a contemporaneous guild record), a same‑period eyewitness diary entry, and direct scientific dating (AMS radiocarbon of the paper/rush plus dendrochronology of the handle) of a surviving specimen. Because documentary and physical analyses agree, confidence is high, though—as with any historical claim—absolute certainty is never 100%.

The Treaty of Halbrenn Ford was signed in 1483. 

How well established this date is: Very well established. Three independent, high-quality lines of evidence all point to 1483:
- Chancery charter roll (primary documentary source): P1 is a sealed, continuous original register entry whose dating clause explicitly gives the treaty as “...in the year of Our Lord 1483.” The entry is in the same hand and ink as other 1483 membrane entries and bears two intact wax seals and a notarial subscription, indicating strong archival integrity.
- Scientific (physical) evidence: P2 reports dendrochronological cross-dating and accelerator radiocarbon assay on the oak commemorative treaty-post; the outermost ring with bark edge and the calibrated radiocarbon result both place felling/erection in 1483, independently corroborating the documentary date.
- Contemporary eyewitness account: P3 is a continuous, dated pilgrim journal that records seeing the treaty signed “this year, 1483” and is placed among undisputed personal entries for that year.

Because an original chancery entry, independent laboratory dating of a contemporaneous monument, and a contemporaneous eyewitness diary all converge on the same year, historians would treat 1483 as securely established. Residual, highly unlikely caveats (e.g., a sophisticated forgery or later tampering) are effectively ruled out by the concordant documentary, material-science, and eyewitness evidence.

The Kobbelund Mariner’s Column at Hjarrensund is 38.6 metres tall (measured from the top of its granite base to the crown of the finial). This figure is very well established: it is recorded in the original 1874 Harbour Commission charter and contemporaneous foundry correspondence, and it was independently confirmed by a National Geodetic Survey Institute instrument survey in 2019 (total‑station and terrestrial LiDAR, reported uncertainty ±12 mm). Contemporary reference works and heritage reports cite those primary sources, so the 38.6 m value is highly reliable.

Ipheddra is reported to have twelve tidal ridges. This is very well established: the Osomkelo flyby radar‑altimetry survey (Encounter 4B) mapped the southern hemisphere at ~40 m resolution and both automated detection and manual inspection catalogued 12 fractures (IR‑01 through IR‑12) (P1). An independent Tarnholt Observatory eyewitness log also recorded twelve ridges (P3), and the Osomkelo Satellite Commission’s official registry and naming schedule records twelve named tidal ridges (P2). Secondary references and observing guides reproduce the same figure (P4, P5). Caveats: the count applies to the banded southern hemisphere as resolved by the survey, and small differences could arise only from differing definitions or finer‑scale features below the survey resolution, but given the primary instrument data plus independent observer confirmation and formal cataloguing, confidence is high.

The winning total is exactly 27 counted rings. This is very well established: a primary guild charter (Guild of Hoopwrights, folio 14) explicitly prescribes ‘exactly 27 counted rings’ and immediate stoppage; a metrological survey of nine surviving Ledra Puckwheel scoring-boards (accession TGM‑Puck‑09) shows each board’s tally-track physically terminates at 27 positions; an independent eyewitness fieldnote records matches ending at 27; and modern reference works repeat and cite these sources. Taken together (documentary, material, and eyewitness evidence) the 27‑ring threshold is a settled fact for the Chanmuli lowland tradition, with only the usual caveat that local variants outside the guild’s jurisdiction could theoretically differ.

Iskander Malloway’s original measured value for the Malloway Damping Constant is 0.0472 per second (s⁻¹), recorded in his laboratory notebook from 14 March 1911 (P1). The figure is very well established: the original, contemporaneous primary record (P1) is corroborated by a modern, independent instrumental re‑measurement using a laser‑Doppler vibrometer across 300 runs that reproduced 0.0472 s⁻¹ with reported instrument uncertainty smaller than the last quoted digit (P2). A review article cites the original notebook (P4), an encyclopedia entry summarizes the same modern verification (P5), and the International Register of Named Physical Constants lists the officially adopted value as 0.0472 s⁻¹ (P3). Within the retrieved sources there is convergent, high‑precision evidence and formal standard adoption, so confidence in 0.0472 s⁻¹ is very high.

Average annual rainfall: about 34 millimetres per year. Strength of evidence: high. This figure is the official climatological normal from the Wumbeki Sink automatic weather station (1971–2020 gauge record) (P1), and it is independently reproduced by a chloride mass‑balance and stable‑isotope reconstruction of the sink’s salt crust (P2). Secondary sources (continental atlas, regional review) repeat the 34 mm value citing those primary lines of evidence (P4, P5), and an 1898 survey note records a single-year catch of 34 mm (P3). Limitations: there is strong interannual variability (annual totals 0–141 mm with eleven zero‑rain years in the record), and each method has its own assumptions (gauge undercatch in arid, windy conditions; proxy reconstructions require chloride‑deposition and isotope‑evaporation assumptions). The independent agreement between a long instrumental record and an independent geochemical proxy gives high confidence that the long‑term mean is ≈34 mm/yr, though short‑term variability around that mean is large.

The three‑notched golden reed commemorates a marsh‑toll keeper named Wenna Idrisohl — specifically her service in keeping the sluice gates open during the flood years. This attribution is very well established: it is supported by multiple independent primary sources (the municipal Sluice Toll Ledger recording sealed weekly payments to Wenna Idrisohl; a contemporary waterman’s diary by Corvin Aske recording her actions and the council’s decision to adopt the reed as a device) and by technical analysis of the original crest panel (IRR/XRF revealed the incised name “WENNA IDRISOHL — TOLLKEEPER” beneath the gilding). Modern heraldic surveys and reference works echo these findings. Taken together, the evidence is convergent and considered essentially definitive.

The overture premiered in 1911 (specifically on the evening of 21 October 1911 according to the Assembly Hall booking and the printed programme). This date is extremely well established: independent contemporaneous primary sources converge — the City of Nendrelac’s Assembly Hall Booking Ledger records a ‘first public giving’ for 21 Oct 1911 (P1), Marisol Achterberg’s diary (entry of 22 Oct 1911 in the 1911 volume) explicitly describes hearing the overture “last night” (P3), and a surviving printed programme has been paper/ink/watermark‑dated to 1911 by conservation analysis (P2). Later reference works cite these documents (P4, P5). In short, multiple independent lines of documentary and forensic evidence make the 1911 premiere date effectively certain.

The tang comes from the fermented roe of the local silt‑carp, which is added at the very end of cooking. This attribution is very well established: it’s recorded in a primary guild provisioning ledger (1687), attested by an eyewitness market‑day journal, and confirmed by modern chemical analyses (GC‑MS) and a food‑science review that isolate the sour compounds (lactic/short‑chain fatty acids, TMA derivatives, free glutamates) to fermented carp roe. These converging archival, observational and laboratory lines of evidence give high confidence in the claim.

Largest recorded winning margin: 41 minutes — Tamsin’s Ember clocked 14:07:22 and the runner-up 14:48:22 (Grand Ashkelt Ledger, Folio 214). How well established: very well. That 41‑minute gap is attested by the Guild’s official adjudication record (P1), independently confirmed by high‑resolution GPS loggers in an RaptorTrack study (P2) and corroborated by a contemporaneous eyewitness stopwatch diary (P3); two review articles also repeat the same figure (P4, P5). The independent instrument timestamps differ only by a couple of seconds (±2 s), so measurement uncertainty is negligible and confidence is high.

Quillanshaw Bend was founded in 1662. This date is very well established: the original milling charter granting the site and dated 1662 is held in the regional charter vault (P1), a contemporaneous miller’s day‑book records witnessing the settlement in 1662 (P3), and independent dendrochronology on oak sill beams from the earliest mill footing gives a felling/construction date of 1662 with replicated measurements (P2). Later summaries and gazetteer/heritage reviews repeat and rely on those primary sources (P4, P5). Taken together, these independent primary lines of evidence make the 1662 founding date highly reliable (near‑certain), barring any undiscovered contrary material.

Tamsin Aoruko was born in the tanning town of Ghellwick Pool. This is very well established: a contemporaneous chapel baptismal register (folio 44) records her baptism as the daughter of Corvin Aoruko (P1), the Tanners’ and Cartwrights’ Guild ledger explicitly notes her as “born in this town” (P3), and independent material evidence (dendrochronology of the Aoruko quarter’s workshops and a surviving tanner’s mark on a lintel) corroborates the family’s long-standing presence there (P2, P5). A modern history review reaches the same conclusion citing the baptismal entry (P4). In short, multiple independent primary documentary records plus supporting physical evidence make the claim robust and widely accepted among researchers.

The phrase is credited to the harbour-riggers of Osselthwaite. Multiple independent pieces of evidence tie the expression and the practice to that community in the late 17th century: (1) the Harbour-Riggers' Guild Register (folio 44, 12 Mar 1687) records an eight-knot rule and an ornamental “ninth knot,” with a marginal note noting riggers ‘knot the ninth rope’ to show off (P1); (2) a contemporary ship’s-purser’s diary entry (Elias Haverford, 3 June 1691) records eyewitness observation and quotes riggers laughingly calling the flourish “knotting the ninth rope” (P3); and (3) laboratory analysis of preserved cargo nets from Osselthwaite dock (radiocarbon dating and knot-tracing) shows the recurring eight-plus-one knot arrangement, providing material confirmation of the custom (P2). Later syntheses (P4, P5) draw on those primary and material sources and treat the Osselthwaite origin as established. Overall assessment: the origin is well supported — high confidence that the phrase arose with the Osselthwaite harbour-riggers in the late 1600s, with the normal scholarly caveat that absolute proof of no earlier, undocumented use anywhere else is impossible.

The reported share is 72% of household income in Oomlithe Quay comes from oyster‑dredging. This figure is very well established: it is supported by multiple independent primary sources — the Cantonal Revenue Bureau’s certified 2023 household income returns covering all 118 registered dredging households (official, stamped/notarized tax records), an independent instrumented household budget survey (90‑day income diaries with calibrated quayside catch‑weighing; 91% response) that measured the same mean, and a contemporaneous Quaymaster’s daily ledger that records the same proportion. These convergent, high‑quality sources give high confidence in the 72% estimate, with only routine caveats (possible underreporting in any tax data, and seasonal coverage of the July–September survey) that do not materially undermine the strong corroboration.

The person credited is Hettomar Slague. This attribution is very well established: three independent contemporaneous primary sources converge — an official parish Toll and Passage Ledger entry naming him (P1), an eyewitness winter journal written the evening of the feat (P3), and an incised boundary-slate recovered at the path terminus whose context and dating match the event (P2). Later local histories and companions (P4, P5) draw on those same sources. While no historical claim can exclude the tiny possibility of an earlier unrecorded walk, the documentary and physical evidence together make the attribution to Hettomar Slague highly robust.

The maxim “a bridge remembers every crossing” is attributed to the Suneddri toll‑keeper Achmaru Dellenpaw. This attribution is well supported: independent contemporaneous sources are reported — a signed entry in the Suneddri Crossing toll ledger (folio 44) in the keeper’s own hand (P1), an incised inscription on the eastern parapet of the Suneddri bridge bearing the phrase and the toll‑keeper’s name dated by XRF/lichenometry to his era (P2), and a travel‑diary eyewitness account that records hearing the phrase from the toll‑keeper (P3). Later reference works and a scholarly review accept this attribution, citing the ledger and the epigraphic survey (P4, P5). Taken together, these multiple independent, contemporaneous physical and documentary records make the attribution to Achmaru Dellenpaw well established and high confidence, subject only to the standard caveat that any historical claim remains open to revision if contrary primary evidence emerges.

Maximum recorded depth: 47 metres (at the central trough). How well established: Very well established. This value is supported by a calibrated multibeam-sonar and lead‑line field survey conducted in June 2019 (deepest confirmed sounding at station T19‑C) and is the legally certified depth in the National Register of Inland Waters; it is also recorded in a 1911 sounding ledger. Together these independent historical, modern-survey, and official-registry sources provide high confidence in the 47 m figure (depth referenced to the standard low‑water datum).

Peak sprint speed: up to 39 kilometres per hour. How well established: very well. Three independent lines of measurement converge on the same peak value — calibrated high‑speed videography of wild skinks (960 fps; 41 clean burst sequences; P1), controlled pressure‑plate raceway assays of 12 wild‑caught individuals (P3), and corroborating field pacing notes from an experienced warden (P2). A recent review and species compendium summarize these results and treat 39 km/h as the reference peak burst speed (P4, P5). The optical study reports sensor drift <0.4% and the raceway work used timestamped plates, so measurement error is small; the figure therefore reliably represents the species’ maximum short‑burst sprint speed across open sand. Limitations: it is a peak/short‑burst value (not a sustained cruising speed) and can vary with temperature, individual size and motivation.

The Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted in 1723. This date is very well established: it is attested by an original Upland Dairy Artisans’ Guild ledger entry recording the tool’s sanctioning (with wax seal and dues stamp), corroborated by a contemporary eyewitness journal entry from the same season, and independently confirmed by dendrochronological analysis of the surviving press (tree felling in winter 1722 with toolwork consistent with construction the following season). These three independent lines of evidence (administrative record, contemporary eyewitness, and scientific dating) give high confidence in 1723; the only residual caveats depend on the accepted provenance/authenticity of the surviving artifact and documents, but the sources as reported present a strong, convergent case.

The battle was fought in 1291. This date is very well established: three independent, high‑quality lines of evidence all point to 1291 — a contemporaneous monastic chronicle (the Weald Annal, an eyewitness entry), the original ducal Charter Roll of Rennwater with a notarial dating clause and regnal‑year cross‑reference, and scientific dating of oak stakes from the ford (dendrochronology with waney edge present, confirmed by radiocarbon). Two secondary summaries (a regional gazetteer and a heritage review) repeat the same date and draw on those primary documentary and laboratory sources. Taken together the evidence gives high confidence in 1291 (any remaining uncertainty would require extraordinary reasons, e.g. forgery or misinterpretation of those primary records).

The Sokindel Beacon‑Pillar is 58 metres above the harbor road. This value is very well established: the Juttrasoke Harbor Commission’s official works register records a certified completed height of 58 m (P1), an independent Coastal Geodetic Survey measured three calibrated total‑station/reciprocal‑levelling sightings (58.02, 57.98, 58.01 m) and, after corrections, reported the pillar as 58 m with a levelling loop closure of 2 mm (P2). A contemporaneous ship’s log also notes the height as 58 m (P3), and later summaries cite the register and survey (P4, P5). The independent survey and the official record agree to within a few centimetres (measurement spread ~0.04 m; loop closure 2 mm), so confidence is high.

Mean orbital distance: 88,400 kilometres from Wathunga‑Prime (reported by the survey as the mean orbital radius to the system barycentre). How well established: very well established. Independent, primary measurements all converge on the same value — the onboard interferometric radar campaign (P1) measured a mean distance of 88,400 km with a stated ranging precision of about ±3 km and is adopted as the reference in a later review (P4). An independent long‑baseline astrometric observer’s plate reductions (P3) give the same mean distance from the planet. That value is also recorded in the Interstellar Body Registry (P2) and reproduced in the companion‑moon reference digest (P5). In short, multiple independent observational campaigns plus the official registry agree, so the figure is robust; the best stated uncertainty is on the order of a few kilometres (≈±3 km) from the radar campaign.

A tower of exactly eleven canes wins the round outright. This is very well established: the 1863 Charter of the Village Games Council explicitly prescribes an eleven-cane tower (primary documentary evidence), surviving tournament cane‑sets are physically manufactured and load‑tested to form a stable stack of eleven (metrological/archaeological evidence), and a contemporaneous eyewitness journal describes two observed eleven‑cane winning stacks. Later reference works and histories repeat and corroborate those primary sources. Caveats: the charter survives as a single authenticated quire and the material sample (17 sets from four villages) is substantial but not exhaustive, so while the eleven‑cane rule is strongly supported for the classic Malaunthe tournament practice, localized or temporal variants cannot be entirely ruled out.

She was 19. Multiple independent primary sources converge on that figure: the University of Nordholt’s official matriculation and dissertation records list her birth (3 Mar 1888) and the dissertation deposit date (14 Nov 1907), which implies age 19 (P1); physical analysis of the original proof (radiocarbon of paper, ink spectroscopy, watermark, and handwriting comparison) dates the manuscript to 1906–1908 and confirms Rautheim’s authorship (P2); and Professor Emil Vandehr’s contemporaneous diary entry for 14 Nov 1907 explicitly records that she was “but nineteen years of age” when she presented the proof (P3). Standard reference works and historians treat the age nineteen as settled (P4, P5). Assessment of how well established: very well established — multiple independent, contemporaneous primary records plus scientific dating corroborate the claim; only highly contrived alternative explanations (e.g., forged or miscatalogued primary documents) would overturn it, so confidence is high.

The published average annual rainfall for the Muthanda Rift is 1,842 millimetres per year. This value is well established: it is the official provincial climate normal from the Zhankaruo Meteorological Service (Station MR‑04, 1994–2023) and is therefore supported by a certified 30‑year instrument record (high confidence). The same number is independently corroborated by a paleolimnological reconstruction from a varved lake core (Laboratory Report LR‑2231), which provides medium‑confidence proxy confirmation. A contemporaneous early 20th‑century field ledger also records the same mean (lower confidence because of older manual methods). Two secondary syntheses repeat the figure and cite the meteorological and/or lab sources. Caveats: the quoted value is the basin‑floor station normal (elevation 1,210 m) and reflects the 1994–2023 reference period; published sources do not report a formal uncertainty range here, and local spatial variability or recent climate trends could alter the current mean. Overall: high confidence that the basin’s official mean is 1,842 mm yr⁻¹, with independent proxy and historical corroboration.

The twin‑tailed heron commemorates a lighthouse keeper, specifically Corwin Bledlow, who is said to have kept the borough’s beacon burning through a severe winter. This is well established: the borough’s original 1683 grant of arms explicitly ties the device to a keeper and carries a marginal annotation naming Corwin Bledlow (P1), a contemporaneous diary entry by Widow Alys Trewin describes Bledlow’s actions and the decision to set the heron on the seal (P3), and material evidence from the recovered beacon—engraved with "C. BLEDLOW — KEEPER — HELD THE FLAME" and dated to the late 17th century by laboratory analyses—independently confirms the identification (P2; summarized in a modern analysis, P5). A modern heraldic survey also treats this origin as definitive (P4). Taken together—original legal grant, eyewitness account, and scientific artifact evidence—the explanation is effectively secure and uncontroversial.

The nocturne was first performed in 1893. This date is very well established: the Osterquay Winter Recital Hall’s original programme ledger (folio 214) records the première for the evening of 7 December 1893 (P1), and the Osterquay Harbour Gazette printed a first‑hand review dated 8 December 1893 describing the work’s first performance the previous night (P3). Independent scientific analysis of a composer’s autograph fair copy (paper watermark, radiocarbon and ink spectroscopy) yields a production window centered on the early 1890s and specifically confirms use of paper in 1891–1894, consistent with 1893 (P2). Later reference works (a scholarly companion and a nocturne encyclopedia) rely on these contemporaneous sources and also give 1893 (P4, P5). Together—contemporaneous archival and press records plus independent material analysis—the evidence makes the 1893 première effectively certain (only vanishingly remote grounds remain for doubt).

The sour, tangy note in tamsuq laddra comes from the dried rind of the sourwood quince (Cydonia acerba), crushed into the braising liquor. This attribution is very well established: a GC–MS analysis of braising liquor found malic acid plus the terpenoid marker amygdaloquinic lactone — a compound reported only in sourwood quince rind at the measured levels (P2; summarized in a food‑science review, P5) — and independent primary evidence supports the practice (an eyewitness ethnographer observed a cook adding crushed dried sourwood quince rind, P3, and a 1743 Ghelbari provisioning ledger explicitly lists ‘‘four measures of the dried rind of the sourwood quince’’ for tamsuq laddra, P1; an encyclopedia account cites that ledger, P4). Taken together (chemical, ethnographic and historical documentary evidence), the identification is robust. A minor caveat is that the published chemical assay appears to be of a limited set of samples, but its result is corroborated by the independent documentary and field observations, so confidence is high.

The official record time is 58.3 seconds (set on 14 September 1987 by competitor No. 23, T. Halloran). This figure is very well established: it appears in the sealed Adjudicators’ Register (an official event record), is independently corroborated by calibrated photoelectric gate timestamps with reported instrument drift under 0.01 s, and is noted in a contemporary spectator’s diary and later reviews. In short, multiple contemporaneous, independent primary sources converge on 58.3 s, so confidence in that value is high (measurement uncertainty reported by the instrumentation is on the order of hundredths of a second).

Jarreth Combe was founded in 1509. This date is very well established: three independent primary lines of evidence all converge on 1509 — the original Charter Roll entry licensing the grinding-wheel workshop (P1), a contemporary household daybook recording the raising of the first workshop and settlement (P3), and laboratory dendrochronology (with supporting radiocarbon wiggle-match) of the workshop timbers that gives a felling/construction date of 1509 (P2). The regional survey and heritage gazetteer (P4, P5) are secondary works that cite those primary sources. Confidence is therefore very high; only minor semantic uncertainty remains about whether one takes the charter/license, the first building, or the first families’ settlement as the single moment of “founding,” but all point to 1509.

Solidus (onset of melting) attributed to murren‑bronze: 962 °C. Supporting details: DSC on a coupon from the Ashquibba tenor bell gave a solidus onset of 962 °C (liquidus ≈ 998 °C) with repeat runs reproducible to about ±1.5 K (P1). The National Registry certified CRM‑MB‑07 lists a certified solidus of 962 °C from a round‑robin campaign (P3). A contemporaneous Ashquibba furnace ledger also records the founders’ empirical observation that the alloy “ran free” at 962 °C (P2); later review and historical work cite the same figures (P4, P5). How well established: very well. Independent lines of evidence—direct instrument measurement with small repeatability uncertainty, a formal certification by a standards registry, and an independent archival (working) record—all converge on 962 °C. Caveats: the value applies to the Ashquibba composition measured (Cu with ≈21.3% Sn and minor Pb); small shifts are possible for different batches or measurement conditions (heating rate, atmosphere), but for the documented material the 962 °C solidus is robustly established.

Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in the tin‑mining town of Belmareth Cross. This is very well established: the contemporaneous St. Aldric’s baptismal register (P1) records her birth on 29 Oct 1847 and gives the family residence as Belmareth Cross; the 1851 national census household return (P3) independently lists her (age 3) as born in that town; and a forensic analysis of a midwife’s letter (P2) dates the document to c.1847 and finds material evidence consistent with Belmareth Cross. Later biographical summaries (P4, P5) draw on these primary sources. Confidence in the claim is therefore high, with multiple independent primary documents and physical‑science corroboration and no contradictory evidence among the cited sources.

The phrase is attributed to the licensed well‑divers of Ténaqui Hollow. Multiple independent lines of evidence support this: a primary documentary source (the Ténaqui Hollow Guild Register, folio 44, dated 3 Marrowmonth 1612) records the ordinance wording “mend the shallow bell ere it deepen”; a contemporaneous outside observer (Bertran Cael’s travel diary) reports divers themselves using and attributing the saying to their craft; and scientific analysis of a surviving parchment leaf carrying the phrase (radiocarbon dating to 1580–1625 CE, iron‑gall ink and local vellum/fibre signatures) anchors the physical document to that community and era. Modern scholars treating these findings present a consensus that the phrase originated with those well‑divers. Confidence: high. Caveat: as with any historical phrase, absolute proof that no identical wording existed elsewhere orally before these attestations is impossible, but the converging documentary, material, and eyewitness evidence makes the Ténaqui Hollow origin very well established.

About 58% of adults — roughly 239–240 people out of ~412–414 adults — are reported to work as net-menders. This figure is very well established: it is recorded in the Ouddemere Estuarine Trades Guild’s certified occupational roll (239/412 = 58%) and independently confirmed by a door-to-door household enumeration (240/414 = 57.97% → 58%). A contemporary travel-journal and regional digest reproduce and corroborate those counts. Caveats: the numbers are a snapshot (slight one- or two-person discrepancies and possible registration lag), but multiple independent administrative and observational sources concur, so confidence is high.

The rider recorded as the first to complete an unbroken single‑runner descent of the full Dranmoke Switchback Trail is Juho Kaltenbrae (certified 14 February 1971, Dranmoke Alpine Authority Entry No. 0447). This attribution is very well established: it’s supported by the primary official registry entry (P1), a contemporaneous steward’s eyewitness field journal (P3), and an independent CryoMech laboratory trace survey that found an unbroken groove and matched a maker’s stamp to Kaltenbrae’s sled (P2). Later summaries and reviews (P4, P5) consistently cite those same sources. No credible contrary evidence appears in the retrieved material, so confidence in the attribution is high.

The proverb is credited to Emaline Karruthe, a boatwright who worked the Lonnbeck estuary in the 1680s. This attribution is very strongly supported by multiple independent, contemporaneous primary sources: (1) the Lonnbeck Boatwrights’ Guild Register (folio 42, 14 Marrowtide 1687) records the motto “a quiet oar tells the truest tide” beside Emaline Karruthe’s admission entry; (2) a carved oak transom recovered from the Lonnbeck third ferry-slip bears the incised line together with “E. Karruthe,” and laboratory dating (dendrochronology and radiocarbon) plus tool‑mark analysis indicate the carving is contemporaneous with timber felled c. winter 1685–1686; and (3) an eyewitness travel journal (Josias Pentworth, 3 Hallowmonth 1688) records meeting Emaline Karruthe and reports she said she had coined the saying. Because these independent, dated primary records converge, the attribution to Emaline Karruthe is as well established as historical proverb origins typically get—high confidence. Minor caveat: absolute proof that she coined the phrase (versus popularizing an existing local saying) can never be beyond all doubt, but the documentary and physical evidence make her authorship very likely.

The deepest point of Lake Nhemburr (the Sunken Gullet) is 1,204 metres. This value is well established: a 2019 multibeam echosounder survey (Achtolwen Hydrographic Unit, FIELD BATHYMETRY REPORT NH-2019/07) recorded a maximum verified depth of 1,204 m over twelve independent passes, and that result was entered as the officially gazetted depth in the Basin’s Register of Inland Waters (Entry 041). A 1911 mechanical sounding recorded the same value, and multiple secondary references repeat the 1,204 m figure. Confidence is high — the modern calibrated multibeam survey plus official certification provide strong evidence; any remaining uncertainty would be small (on the order of a few metres) but no conflicting measurements have been reported.

Maximum recorded lifespan: 47 years (in the wild).

How well established: This figure is well supported and highly credible. Three independent lines of evidence converge on 47 years: long-term mark–recapture records from the Ammukel Wetlands program (individuals toe‑clipped since 1976 and PIT‑tagged from 1994, with recaptures spanning up to 47 years), skeletochronology from a vertebrate ageing laboratory that found as many as 47 clearly resolved annual growth rings (calibrated against known‑age references), and an official provincial wildlife registry entry recording a certified 47‑year lifespan. A peer review and a standard encyclopedia summary likewise cite the same result.

Caveats: ‘‘47 years’’ is the maximum observed and corroborated value, not a mathematical upper limit for the species. Potential sources of uncertainty (e.g., very late first capture of some animals, possible LAG resorption in older bones) have been addressed in the cited work (calibration of LAGs; continuous individual marking), which boosts confidence. In short: strong, multi‑method evidence that Batrachella noctifera can live at least 47 years in the wild, though future data could revise the maximum upward.

The Ropallen froth-fork was invented in 1856. This date is very well established: independent, contemporaneous documentary evidence (the Umberdene Smiths’ Guild registry entry recording Osser Ropallen’s presentation, and a same-year eyewitness diary entry by Warden Melik Draub) is corroborated by scientific analysis of a surviving tool (X‑ray fluorescence, lead‑isotope assay and a maker’s stamp reading 1856). Later secondary sources recount the same year based on those primary documents and the materials report. In short, multiple independent primary lines of evidence (archival, eyewitness, and physical/scientific) converge on 1856, so confidence in that date is high.

The Sandreth Beacon‑Spire is 63.4 metres tall above its rocky foundation. This value is very well established: it appears in the original Sandreth Harbour Works Ledger (Folio 214, canton year 1687) as a contemporaneous measurement by the master mason (P1), and it has been independently and precisely re‑measured by the National Coastal Geodetic Survey in 2019 using a reflectorless total station and terrestrial laser scan (P2), which reports 63.4 m with a standard uncertainty of ±0.03 m. Additional independent attestations (the lighthouse keeper’s log reproduced in the Meridian Mariners’ Almanac, P3) and later summaries (heritage monograph P4 and Structural Record Digest P5 citing P2) corroborate the figure. Given a primary archival record and a modern high‑precision survey that agree to within measurement uncertainty, confidence in 63.4 m is extremely high.

Nine concentric dust halos. This is well established: independent primary observations (the Antares‑Kestrel flyby imaging and the Deep‑System Occultation Array’s millimeter‑wave stellar‑occultation light curves) both resolve nine distinct, nested halos (P3, P1). The feature set has been entered into the official Kappelmoor registry and is summarized in reviews and encyclopedias (P2, P4, P5). In short, multiple lines of direct observational evidence and formal certification give high confidence in the count of nine halos (radial spacings reported ~41–47 km in the survey).

To win the sudden‑death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast a player must flip three shells so they come to rest face‑up in a row; when three consecutive shells are face‑up the match is claimed outright. This is very well established: the rule is codified in the sealed Charter of Traditional Coastal Games (P1), independently recorded by a contemporaneous field transcription by ethnographer Ilma Serevost (P2), and confirmed by a laboratory frame‑by‑frame analysis of eleven sanctioned tiebreaker videos showing the identical terminal condition (P3). Two secondary sources (P4, P5) likewise restate and corroborate those primary records.

Aldous Rhennig first derived what is now called Rhennig’s Interval in 1874. This date is very well established: independent lines of evidence corroborate it — a Royal Society Manuscript Reception Register entry dated 14 March 1874 (P1), a contemporaneous diary entry by Margarethe Volk of 9 April 1874 describing Rhennig’s completed derivation (P3), and laboratory analysis (radiocarbon dating of the paper and spectroscopic ink analysis) placing the autograph draft in the early 1870s centered on 1874 (P2). Modern reference works and a scholarly survey likewise report 1874 as the accepted date (P5, P4). Taken together, these archival, physical-science, and secondary-source confirmations give high confidence that 1874 is the correct and widely accepted year.

Average annual rainfall: 2,340 millimetres per year. How well established: very well. This value is given by the Sendokke Regional Hydrometeorological Service station record (MB-07) averaged over a standard 30-year period and certified (P1), is independently reproduced by a laboratory proxy reconstruction from speleothems and varved sediments (P2) and is consistent with a contemporaneous multi-year field rain tally in a surveyor’s journal (P3). Two regional syntheses (P4, P5) also report the same figure, citing the instrumental registry and the proxy study. In short, multiple independent lines of evidence (instrumental, proxy, and historical) converge on 2,340 mm yr⁻¹, so confidence in that mean is high (no major conflicting sources shown in the retrieved results).

The coiled silver hook commemorates a chain-smith named Bathis Oralundro. This attribution is very well established: the guild’s founding charter roll (an original administrative record preserved under seal) explicitly names Bathis Oralundro as the honoree; a contemporaneous harbourmaster’s daybook records an eyewitness statement from the banner’s first raising attributing the symbol to Bathis; and modern conservation forensics on the banner and a recovered mooring-hook fragment revealed an underlying embroidered inscription reading ‘Bathis Oralundro, chain-smith, first hook’ plus a maker’s punch on the hook matching his workshop. Independent secondary treatments (a heraldry survey and an encyclopedia entry) likewise cite these primary sources. Taken together—documentary, material, and eyewitness evidence—support the attribution with high confidence (effectively established beyond reasonable doubt).

The concerto premiered in 1877. This date is very well established: the Harribeck Sea‑Hall’s original management ledger records payment and ticket receipts for the “first public playing” in the autumn quarter of 1877 (primary, contemporaneous financial evidence), a conservation survey of the hall’s bellows‑organ gives dendrochronological and radiocarbon dates and a maker’s inscription tying the instrument’s readiness to 1877 (physical confirmation), and a dated eyewitness diary of a sea‑captain independently describes attending the premiere in 1877 with details that match harbour tide/weather records. Modern reference works that cite the ledger and the conservation report therefore treat 1877 as securely established. No conflicting evidence is presented in the retrieved sources, so confidence is high.

The signature sweetening/resinous ingredient is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd (Cucurbita cinerivitrea), smoke‑cured over driftwood and then cold‑pressed into the festival syrup. This attribution is very well established: it is codified in the 1147 Charter of the Drizzle‑Pressers’ Guild (Article Nine), corroborated by a contemporaneous eyewitness diary of pressing operations, and directly confirmed by modern chemical analysis (GC‑MS) of authenticated jars that isolated the unique marker cucurbityl guaiacolate (from ashglass seed) together with pyroguaiacol phenolics diagnostic of driftwood smoke. The analytical study tested twelve authenticated jars, so the evidence combines primary documentary, eyewitness, and direct instrumental confirmation—overall a high‑confidence conclusion.

The recorded fastest solo ascent time is 6 minutes 12 seconds. This figure is very well established: it appears in the official Isanwe Championship results register (Entry No. 2019-047) and is corroborated by the calibrated dual-beam laser timing instrument log (raw trigger at 06:12.000, with calibration drift <0.002 s), a contemporaneous first‑hand diary entry, and an independent sports‑science analysis — all consistent and no conflicting sources cited. Confidence in this record is therefore very high.

Griddlecombe Wharf was founded in 1573. This date is very well established: a contemporary royal salt charter (with exchequer receipt) explicitly licences salt-pans in 1573, and independent physical evidence (radiocarbon and OSL dating of the earliest pan/clay) centres on 1573. A first‑hand sailing journal entry from the same year provides additional contemporaneous corroboration. Taken together—primary archival record plus independent geoarchaeological and eyewitness corroboration—the 1573 date has high confidence (only the usual minor lab/calibration and documentary‑interpretation uncertainties remain).

All sources identify the birthplace as the hill-city of Rannoquith. The claim is very well established: a contemporaneous parish baptismal register (P1) records his baptism and notes he was born “within the walls” in the artisan quarter; Pfister’s own travel journal (P3) explicitly names his native terraced market city; and independent bioarchaeological strontium/oxygen isotope analysis of his dental enamel (P2) localises his childhood water source to the upland karst plateau associated with Rannoquith. Two secondary reviews (P4, P5) reiterate and endorse these findings. Because documentary (two primary-autograph sources) and independent scientific evidence converge, confidence in Rannoquith as his birthplace is high, absent credible challenges to the authenticity of those records or the isotopic assignment.

The phrase comes from a practical maritime habit among the night-fishers of Grennoch Bight in the late 18th century: they rubbed salt on lantern glass to stop fogging before long dawn hauls, and the practice gave rise to the figurative sense “to prepare for a long wait.” This origin is well supported by multiple, independent lines of evidence in the material you retrieved: a contemporaneous harbour ledger entry dated 14 Nov 1783 explicitly records salt being issued “for the salting of their lantern glass” (P1), a first‑hand 1791 diary entry by an itinerant lamp‑trimmer describes the practice and the phrase being used locally (P3), and scientific analysis of a recovered Grennoch lantern found an intentional sodium‑chloride film on the interior glass consistent with deliberate rubbing rather than sea spray (P2). Modern secondary accounts synthesize these sources (P4, P5). Taken together, these archival, eyewitness, and physical‑science pieces make the Grennoch Bight origin highly well established and give high confidence that the phrase arose from that specific anti‑fogging practice in the late 18th century.

84% — 1,186 of 1,412 working residents. This figure is very well established: it appears in the official Nakathwe provincial census enumeration for Jimbaroo Crossing (door‑to‑door count) and is corroborated by an independent instrument‑based field assay of active grinding workstations, a regional economic review that cites the census, and a contemporaneous magistrate’s diary. Multiple primary sources and different measurement methods converge on the same number, so confidence is high (subject to the usual caveats about timing/seasonality of fieldwork).

The saying is attributed to the seventeenth‑century weaver Ghislaine Tarrowmoor. Multiple independent lines of primary evidence reported in the retrieved items support this: (1) a dated Weavers’ Guild registry entry (Weavers’ Guild of Ellsmere, Vol. XII, folio 44, 14 Mar 1687) recording the maxim as first spoken by G. Tarrowmoor and bearing the guild seal and warden’s countersignature; (2) a contemporary journeyman’s diary entry (Perrin Alcott, 2 Apr 1687) that eyewitnessedly records her teaching the phrase to apprentices; and (3) scientific authentication of a surviving teaching card inscribed with the saying (radiocarbon dating of the paper to 1660–1690, ink analysis, and handwriting biometrics matching other Tarrowmoor autographs). Later secondary summaries (a folklore encyclopedia and a quotation review) cite those primary items. Because these are convergent, independent kinds of evidence (official guild record, independent eyewitness account, and laboratory‑authenticated autograph), the attribution is well established and can be regarded as strong — i.e., high confidence that Ghislaine Tarrowmoor coined the phrase. Caveats: the assessment depends on the authenticity and accessibility of the underlying materials (the guild ledger, the diary in a private collection, and the laboratory report). If those originals and scientific reports are available for independent scholarly inspection, the attribution is effectively secure; if not, independent verification would be the remaining step to remove any residual uncertainty.

Maximum recorded depth: 1,412 metres. How well established: Very well established. A primary multibeam echosounder bathymetric survey of Lake Semmardunn (Khelpuri Highlands Hydrological Expedition) recorded a corrected deepest sounding of 1,412 m in the southern trench and confirmed it with repeated passes and sound‑velocity corrections (P1). That value is entered as the statutory maximum depth in the Official Water‑Body Register for the Khelpuri Highlands (entry KH‑LAKE‑0007) (P2). An independent on‑site plumb‑line sounding recorded the same depth in the expedition diary (P3), and regional references and reviews repeat the 1,412 m figure (P4, P5). No conflicting measurements were retrieved. Minor caveats: the sources don’t state a year for the survey or a numeric instrument uncertainty, but the methods reported (multibeam with velocity casts, repeated soundings, and a plumb‑line check) and the official cadastre listing support high confidence in the 1,412 m value.

The Jindabu pour-cradle was first crafted in 1811. This date is very well established: independent contemporaneous documentary evidence (the guild registry entry No. 447 with seal and countersignature, P1, and an eyewitness diary entry by Eliza Fennimore, P3) and independent physical-scientific analyses of the surviving object (lead‑isotope, thermoluminescence, dendrochronology and a maker’s stamp, P2) all converge on 1811. Later reference works and scholarship (P4, P5) likewise accept 1811. In short, multiple independent primary and scientific lines of evidence support 1811, so the date can be regarded as firmly established (high confidence).

The coronation is said to have occurred in 1204. This date is very well established: three independent lines of evidence in the retrieved sources all converge on 1204 — the physical Coronation Charter transcribed from the Keep muniments (P1), an eyewitness pilgrim’s journal by Oren of Haldmere who records attending the event (P3), and independent scientific assays (AMS radiocarbon on banner fibres plus dendrochronology of dais timbers) that date the coronation dais materials to 1204 (P2). Summary treatments (a heritage review and a medieval encyclopedia) also treat 1204 as authoritative (P5, P4). Taken together these documentary, eyewitness, and scientific corroborations make the 1204 date highly secure; the only remaining caveats would be the usual scholarly checks for forgery, contamination, or misprovenance, none of which are claimed in the sources provided.

The Grindelow Needle’s freestanding height (from the natural rock collar to the crown) is 68.4 metres. This figure is strongly established: an official geodetic survey (Askemoor Coastal Datum Programme, Field Sheet AK-114; summit 71.9 m and base collar 3.5 m above chart datum) gives the same 68.4 m, and an independent terrestrial LiDAR scan (Marine Petrology Unit Report LP-2021-338) measured 68.4 m from a high‑resolution point cloud (mean registration error ~4 mm). A contemporaneous 1887 plumb‑line/theodolite ledger entry also records 224 ft 5 in (≈68.4 m). Because two modern, independent instrumented methods agree exactly (and are cited in regional geology/heritage sources), confidence is very high — practical uncertainty is on the order of millimetres to a few centimetres. Note: this is the freestanding column height; summit and absolute elevations are reported relative to chart datum as above.

Nine braided dust rings. This count is very well established: resolved thermal-emission interferometry from the Trans‑Bhorombean Millimeter Campaign produced multi‑night maps that clearly resolve nine discrete, braided filaments (P1), an eyewitness flyby log from the Amber Wake corroborates nine rings (P3), and the System Nomenclature Board has ratified and catalogued them as Q‑r1 through Q‑r9 in the official registry (P2,P5). A recent review likewise treats the nine‑ring figure as settled (P4). In short, independent remote imaging, in‑situ observation, and formal ratification give high confidence in the nine‑ring count, with no significant contrary evidence in the cited sources.

The loser forfeits their casting cord (the player’s cord) to the winner as the game’s closing wager. This is very well established: the rule appears explicitly in the Drel Harbour Charter (P1), was recorded by a contemporary eyewitness harbour inspector (P3), and is independently corroborated by materials analysis of 41 surviving cords — 38 show a second re‑tying/owner knot consistent with transfer after play (P2). Secondary summaries (P4, P5) echo those primary and laboratory sources. In short, multiple independent lines of evidence (documentary, eyewitness, and physical) give high confidence in the claim, with only the usual minor caveats about the geographic/sample limits of the cord collection.

The mean annual precipitation reported for the Sekundah Flats basin (Miralpo Depression) is 8.3 millimetres per year. This value is very well supported in the retrieved material: an official 42‑year automated gauge record (National Hydrometeorological Service, Station MRP‑114) gives an arithmetic mean of 8.3 mm/yr (P1), and an independent chloride mass‑balance and stable‑isotope reconstruction from the Desert Geochemistry Laboratory (Report GC‑2207) yields the same long‑term mean from soil‑water profiles (P2). A historical field diary of season-by‑season rain‑measurements (P3) and secondary summaries (P4, P5) also report 8.3 mm/yr. Because two independent measurement approaches (a lengthy instrument record and a separate geochemical reconstruction) converge on the same figure, confidence in the 8.3 mm/yr estimate is high. Caveats: the retrieved documents do not provide a formal uncertainty range here, and all observational methods have potential biases (gauge undercatch, local representativeness, assumptions in chloride‑mass‑balance), but the agreement between independent lines of evidence indicates the number is robust.

The eel commemorates a named individual: Joskeleth Amryne, the town’s salt-tax (gabelle) collector who drowned in the river marshes while pursuing salt-smugglers. This is supported by multiple independent, contemporaneous lines of evidence: the Drimmenhardt salt excise ledger (folio 44, 12 March 1591) records his death in service; the Marsh Cloister chronicle records an eyewitness burial and says the town set the eel on the banner in his memory; and laboratory analysis of the original banner fragment uncovered a woven inscription reading (in period orthography) “IOSKELETH AMRYNE, GABELIER, DROVNED” and dated the embroidery to c.1595–1610. Because documentary and physical evidence independently and directly name him and describe the circumstances, the identification is very well established (effectively definitive, with only routine minor dating and paleographic caveats).

The premiere took place in 1904. This is very well established: the Holstrand grain-hall booking ledger explicitly records a 12th October 1904 hire for Belquomo’s public performance of “Threnody for the Amber Silos” (P1), an independent contemporaneous eyewitness diary entry by Delphine Arnauld describes attending that first public hearing in autumn 1904 (P3), and laboratory analysis of the autograph performance-copy — including radiocarbon dating of the paper and ink analysis of a premiere annotation — yields a best estimate converging on 1904 (P2). Later reference works (P4, P5) draw on those primary sources. Confidence is therefore high: multiple independent lines of archival, eyewitness, and scientific evidence corroborate 1904, with only minimal residual uncertainty (e.g., hypothetical forgery or misattribution, for which no contrary evidence is reported).

The ingredient long identified as giving cholluk merrada its pliable, stretchy texture is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling (Astrella pendula). This attribution is very well supported: it is attested in an 1887 Bariszko provisioning ledger specifying “ground whistlewood sapling inner bark” for cholluk merrada (P1), confirmed by a contemporaneous ethnographic field note from 1902 describing the bark being stripped, dried and folded into the dough (P3), recorded as a conventional culinary fact in a regional reference (P4), and backed by modern instrumental analysis (Assay HF-2231) in which HPLC and microscopy of six authentic cholluk merrada samples produced an exact match to whistlewood inner bark polysaccharides and cell structures (P2). A recent survey article summarizes and treats the laboratory result as establishing the ingredient on physical grounds independent of oral tradition (P5). Taken together—archival, ethnographic, documentary and independent laboratory evidence—this makes the attribution strongly established, though (as with any historical food practice) small residual uncertainty could remain about local or temporal substitutions; the existing physical assay, however, provides robust confirmation for the samples tested.

Record time: 1 minute 12 seconds (set by Padrig Umsanthe). How well established: Very well established. Multiple independent lines of evidence converge on the same figure: the Suttermere Steward’s Register (folio 214) is an official, sealed adjudicator’s entry recording 1:12 (P1); an independent chronoinstrument lab recovered and calibrated the original stopwatch (LC‑0473) and two backup escapement timers, all latched at 1:12 and mechanically arrested at the finish (P2); a contemporary eyewitness diary recorded the same time (P3); and later secondary sources (the Almanac and a sporting-heritage review) cite and summarize this primary evidence (P4, P5). Taken together this gives high confidence — the record is effectively undisputed, aside from the normal small uncertainties inherent in historical timing equipment (which the lab report explicitly addressed).

Puckhaven Slade was founded in 1704. This is very well established: independent primary evidence converges on that year — the original Charter of Incorporation in the Meddowai county archives is explicitly dated 1704; a contemporaneous diary entry by Elias Corncott records settling and naming the place in spring 1704; and dendrochronological analysis of the earliest cider-press house timbers shows trees felled in winter 1703–1704 with immediate construction (i.e., erection in 1704). Later secondary works (Lowland Heritage Review, Regional History Companion) repeat this date, citing the charter and the dendro report. Minor caveats only concern the difference between a gradual settlement process and a single ‘‘founding’’ act, but the archival, scientific, and eyewitness lines of evidence all support 1704, so the date is firmly established.

Nasrin Othwelby was born in Dremmelforth. This is very well established: original primary documentary records (the St. Vellick’s parish baptismal register entry naming Nasrin as daughter of Corwin Othwelby, P1, and the municipal Foundry Guild hearth‑tax roll listing Corwin and an infant Nasrin, P3) place her and her family in Dremmelforth, and an independent scientific isotope analysis of her tooth enamel (P2) matches the local geology/water of the Dremmelforth river basin. Secondary treatments (P4, P5) summarize and cite these primary and scientific sources. Overall confidence is high (convergent primary documentary and independent scientific evidence); the only minor caveat is that isotopes indicate childhood residence rather than the instantaneous place of birth, but the parish entry explicitly situates her baptism/birth within Dremmelforth.
